title: Burst-decay probe scratchpad
content:
Goal: quick iterative notes on behaviour when an ingress spike decays (burst->steady). I want to capture: (1) what latency modes appear during decay, (2) how KV cache and cold paths influence tail, (3) whether we can shape cheap infra knobs (min-instances, pre-warm) to reduce p99 without overspending.

Environment:
- model: opt-6.7b-quant8 (local quantized runner build)
- runtime: serving-runtime v0.9.1-rc3 (kernel selection patch applied)
- instance: g4dn.12xlarge-equivalent emulation (8xA100-local in lab)
- concurrency per instance: 16 active requests
- batcher: continuous-batcher with max-batch-ms=8, min-batch=1
- KV cache: enabled with 5-minute prefix TTL
- client: k6 script + custom ramp-down generator (see cmd below)

Traffic pattern (scripted):
- t0..10s: spike to 500 QPS (poisson-ish), mean payload ~150 tokens
- t10..70s: exponential decay to 50 QPS, half-life ~15s (not linear)
- t70..end: steady 50 QPS for 3 minutes
- run length: 4 minutes, repeated 3x per config

Commands (notes to self):
- k6: k6 run --vus 500 --duration 4m burst-decay.js (but we use custom generator)
- bench harness: ./bench/run_ramp --pattern burst-decay --seed 42 --out csv/runA.csv

Key metrics to capture: p50, p90, p95, p99, success_rate, tokens/s, instances_active, batch_size_distribution, kvcache_hit_rate

Experiment matrix (quick):
A) warm-cache (primed with 200 warm requests) + min-instances=2
B) cold-cache (no priming) + min-instances=2
C) cold-cache + min-instances=0 (scale-from-0)
D) warm-cache + min-instances=4 + batcher.max-batch-ms=2 (aggressive burst coalescing)

Results (aggregated summary, single-run median of 3 repeats):
- Run A (warm, min=2): achieved peak throughput 480 QPS, p50=34ms, p95=112ms, p99=280ms, success=99.98%, kvcache_hit_rate=0.87, mean_batch_size_peak=10
- Run B (cold, min=2): peak throughput 460 QPS, p50=38ms, p95=190ms, p99=740ms (big spike at t0..8s), success=99.92%, kvcache_hit_rate=0.12 initially -> 0.78 after 30s, mean_batch_size_peak=9
- Run C (cold, min=0): scaled up slower, effective throughput only 320 QPS during first 20s, p50=55ms, p95=420ms, p99=1400ms, instances ramped from 0->6 over 18s (observed cold spinup penalty)
- Run D (warm, min=4, max-batch-ms=2): peak throughput 500 QPS, p50=28ms, p95=98ms, p99=210ms, success=99.99%, mean_batch_size_peak=12 (coalescing helped), slightly higher steady cost (2.1x tokens/sec cost vs A)

Observations / notes:
- Cold-cache penalty dominates early tail. Even with min-instances=2 the first 8-12s show p99 blowups (Run B). This is mostly KV cache miss + model kv initialization + kernel lazy compile GC spikes.
- Scale-from-0 is unacceptable for bursty short-lived spikes; scale-from-0 leads to both lost throughput and extreme tail (Run C). If customer patterns include occasional sub-1min spikes we should recommend min-instances >0.
- Aggressive coalescing (lower max-batch-ms) helped p95/p99 slightly while increasing mean batch size — seems counterintuitive but reduced per-token scheduling overhead on hot path. Need to validate more runs with varied sequence lengths.
- Warm priming (200 requests) is cheap and reduces p99 by ~2.6x in this workload. Consider a small warm-prefill for new model versions and after long idle windows.
- There are still stochastic p99 spikes around t~15-25s in some repeats — correlate with host-level CPU steal and kernel JIT events. Attach system-profiler next time.

Quick diagnostic traces to collect next runs:
- instance-level perf counters (cpu, ctx-switches, iowait) with 1s resolution
- runtime traces: kvcache.Miss events, kernel-compile.start/finish, batch.dispatch timestamps
- network egress/ingress to rule out proxy-level buffering (nginx/ envoy)

Immediate actionables:
- Add a "burst-prefill" flag in the autoscaler that executes N warm requests when min-instances > 0 and model version changes. (JIRA-INF-823)
- Add a short-lived pre-warm hook to runtime to force-kick kernel compile for hot layers for the first epoch (script in linked PR).
- Instrument batcher to log per-batch origin (burst vs steady) to understand coalescing behavior during decay.

Hypotheses to validate:
1) The majority of p99 early in decay is KV miss + kernel compile; remove either and p99 collapses.
2) Scaling latency (instance spinup) explains Run C loss more than cold-model cost — need better profiling of instance startup path.
3) A tiny always-on pool (1-2 instances) + tiny prefill reduces p99 dramatically at modest cost.

Next experiments (short list):
- Repeat matrix with >=5 repeats and capture full traces (cpu/perf + runtime events).
- Run same matrix but vary payload length (50, 150, 400 tokens) to check token-amortized warmup cost.
- Test with different quant levels (int8 vs int4 fallback) to see compile variance.

Notes to self (TODO):
- Attach raw CSVs to PR and link to chart (done to repo but need to link here).
- Add a small grafana dashboard snapshot for burst decay visualization.
- Share findings in standup and propose "burst-prefill" RFC next week.

Rough sketch of CSV snippet (time, qps, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, instances, kvcache):
2024-03-18T12:00:01Z,480,32,110,270,3,0.85
2024-03-18T12:00:05Z,475,33,115,300,3,0.82
2024-03-18T12:00:12Z,420,40,130,520,3,0.27
2024-03-18T12:00:25Z,200,44,160,700,4,0.48

If I had to summarize in one line: for short decaying bursts, a small warm pool + a 200-request prefill is the highest ROI to reduce early tail without massively increasing steady cost.

End of notes.
